definition: A term referring to the most advanced, highest-capability AI models available at a given point in time, typically large foundation models pushing the boundary of what AI systems can do.
details: Frontier models are often subject to additional safety testing and evaluation given their novel and less well-understood capabilities compared to smaller, more established models.

explainer.lead: “Frontier model” is a moving label for the AI models at the leading edge of capability, not a permanent rank or a particular size. It matters because these systems can do new things whose risks are not yet well understood, so their release often calls for extra testing and evaluation.

tiers.eli5: Think of a race where the leading runners change as the race continues. A frontier model is like one of today’s leaders: it can do some of the most advanced things AI can do right now, but another model may take its place later.
tiers.practitioner: Use the term as a time-dependent comparison, and record which model version and point in time you mean. When deploying such a model, plan for additional safety testing and evaluation rather than assuming that results from smaller, established models transfer cleanly. A common pitfall is treating impressive capability as evidence that failure modes are already well characterized.
tiers.paperLevel: At time t, the frontier can be written as F(t) = the set of available models with the highest overall demonstrated capability, usually large foundation models extending the current performance boundary. There is no fixed capability threshold: membership changes as stronger models appear, and novel capabilities may carry less well-understood risks.

explainer.example: Suppose a lab releases a large general-purpose model that performs tasks beyond the abilities of currently available systems. The team treats it as a frontier model and conducts additional safety evaluation; when a substantially more capable successor appears, the frontier label shifts toward the newer leading systems.

usedIn.name: Foundation model development
usedIn.detail: Used to distinguish models that are extending the current limits of AI capability.

usedIn.name: AI safety evaluation
usedIn.detail: Used to identify systems whose novel capabilities warrant additional testing.

usedIn.name: Model release planning
usedIn.detail: Used when deciding how much evaluation a highly capable, less-understood system needs before deployment.

explainer.intuition: The frontier is the moving edge of what AI can currently do. Models near that edge are often both unusually capable and unusually uncertain, because there is less experience with their behavior.
howItWorks: Compare the general-purpose AI models available at a particular time.
Identify those demonstrating the highest capabilities or new kinds of performance.
Call that leading group the current frontier rather than assigning a permanent title.
Apply additional safety testing because their behavior may be less well understood.
Revise the label as more capable models become available.
explainer.whyItMatters: The term focuses attention on both capability and uncertainty at the same time. It supports extra scrutiny for systems whose novel behavior cannot be fully understood from experience with older models.
misconceptions: Frontier is not a permanent model name or certification.
It does not mean every capability is superior in every situation.
Advanced performance does not imply that the risks are fully understood.
